summary: Defines an optional, transitive BGP attribute for announcing BGP Prefix Segment Identifiers, which are used by Segment Routing. It also specifies how receiving routers process it, so Segment Routing can be used where BGP carries the labels.

eli5.summary: This adds a small tag to BGP messages that says which numbered signpost belongs to a destination, so paths can be built from signposts.

questions: what is the bgp prefix-sid attribute
what is a label index in segment routing
subtitle: A BGP attribute that hands out a numbered label index for each prefix, so Segment Routing can run over BGP in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing needs every prefix to have a network-wide identifier (a Prefix-SID), and BGP had no way to carry one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8669 defines the optional, transitive BGP Prefix-SID attribute (type code 40). It carries a Label-Index TLV that each router turns into a local MPLS label, plus an optional Originator SRGB TLV.
tldr.outcome: Routers can build Segment Routing paths using BGP Labeled Unicast, with strict rules for ignoring, logging and containing bad or conflicting attributes inside one administrative domain.

today: RFC 8669 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the attribute for MPLS Labeled Unicast only, and the text leaves other address families and IPv6 data plane use to future specifications.

sections.title: What a BGP Prefix-SID Is
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) steers traffic with a list of instructions called segments, each named by a Segment Identifier (SID). On the MPLS data plane, a SID is a label. A BGP Prefix Segment is a BGP prefix with a Prefix-SID attached. It is always a global SID within the SR domain, and it means: forward the packet over the Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) best path that BGP computed to that prefix.

This RFC defines the BGP Prefix-SID attribute and the rules to originate it, receive it and handle errors. It applies to Multiprotocol BGP IPv4/IPv6 Labeled Unicast (RFC 8277). Other address family combinations are not defined here, and Segment Routing over IPv6 is out of scope. Example use cases are in RFC 8670, and the architecture is in RFC 8402.

One cost is noted: because a Prefix-SID is attached to a single prefix, each prefix is advertised individually, which reduces how well BGP can pack advertisements that share attributes.
sections.eli5: Each destination gets a number that works like a signpost. BGP carries the signposts so every router in the network knows them.

sections.title: Label Indexes and the SRGB
sections.content:
The operator gives each locally originated prefix a globally unique label index, written L_I, and it is advertised to all other BGP speakers in the SR domain. Each speaker has a label block called the Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB). The SRGB is a local property, so it can differ between speakers, although RFC 8402 recommends using the same one everywhere.

A speaker derives its local label L from the index and its own SRGB, as described in RFC 8660, and programs that label as the incoming label for the prefix. The outgoing label still comes from the NLRI of the Labeled Unicast advertisement, so the label index is only a hint for choosing the local label.

To put a prefix segment into a label stack for traffic engineering, you need the originator's SRGB. The RFC prefers BGP-LS for collecting that information, and offers the Originator SRGB TLV as an optional alternative that does not support traffic engineering.
sections.eli5: Every town hands out the same house numbers, but each one adds its own starting offset to turn a number into a street address. The index is the number, and the SRGB is the offset.

sections.title: The Attribute and Its TLVs
sections.content:
The BGP Prefix-SID attribute is an optional, transitive BGP path attribute, and IANA assigned it type code 40. It is a set of Type/Length/Value (TLV) tuples, each starting with a 1-octet type and a 2-octet length. Unknown TLVs MUST be ignored and propagated unmodified.

The Label-Index TLV (type 1, length 7) holds an 8-bit RESERVED field, 16 bits of Flags (none defined) and a 32-bit Label Index. Reserved and Flags MUST be clear on transmission and ignored on reception. It MUST be present on IPv4/IPv6 Labeled Unicast prefixes and is ignored for other address families.

The Originator SRGB TLV (type 3) is optional. Its value is 16 bits of Flags (none defined) followed by one or more SRGB entries. Each entry is 3 octets for the first label of a range and 3 octets for the number of labels. Several entries are concatenated into one SRGB. This TLV MUST NOT be changed while the update propagates. If a speaker has the same node's SRGB from BGP-LS and from this TLV, the values should match; if not, the BGP-LS values SHOULD be preferred and an error logged.
sections.eli5: The note on each message is a little form with labeled boxes. One box holds the destination's number, and another optional box says what range of numbers its owner uses.

sections.title: Receiving and Advertising
sections.content:
A speaker that gets the attribute from an EBGP neighbor outside the SR domain MUST discard it unless configured to accept it. For Labeled Unicast, the attribute MUST contain the Label-Index TLV, and one without it is "invalid".

The derived label is L = L_I + SRGB_Start. An attribute is conflicting if the derived label falls outside the speaker's SRGB, or if different prefixes arrive with the same label index (all of them are then conflicting). Otherwise it is acceptable. If the best path's attribute is acceptable, the speaker SHOULD program the derived label for the prefix. For invalid or conflicting attributes, it MUST ignore the attribute and allocate an ordinary dynamic label. A conflicting attribute SHOULD NOT be treated as an error and SHOULD be propagated unchanged, with a warning logged.

The outgoing label is always taken from the NLRI. For example, with an Implicit NULL label the speaker MUST pop the top label as usual.

When advertising, a speaker SHOULD pass on an acceptable attribute unmodified. An originator attaches the attribute with a configured label index, and the NLRI Label field MUST be the local label programmed for the prefix. By default it SHOULD NOT advertise the attribute outside its AS, and filtering SHOULD remove it at the domain boundary.
sections.eli5: When a router gets a number it checks whether it fits in its own range. If it fits, it uses it. If it does not fit, it ignores the number and picks any free one, like a normal router would.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
A malformed or invalid attribute on a Labeled Unicast prefix MUST be ignored and not advertised to other peers. Malformed means it cannot be parsed: it is shorter than the minimum, a TLV length breaks that TLV's constraints, or a TLV length runs past the end of the attribute. This is the "Attribute discard" action from RFC 7606, and the speaker SHOULD log an error.

If the attribute appears more than once in an UPDATE, every occurrence after the first is discarded and processing continues. If a recognized TLV that may appear only once shows up repeatedly, the extra copies are discarded in the same way.

Because conflicts are not treated as errors, a mis-set label index does not bring down the session. The prefix simply falls back to a normal dynamic label.
sections.eli5: If a note is scribbled so badly it cannot be read, the router throws that note away and carries on with the rest of the message.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned attribute type 40 to the BGP Prefix-SID attribute and created a "BGP Prefix-SID TLV Types" registry. Values 1 to 254 are by Expert Review, and 0 and 255 are reserved. Type 1 is Label-Index and type 3 is Originator SRGB. Type 2 is deprecated: it was the IPv6 SID TLV from earlier drafts, and IPv6 data plane use was deferred to future specifications.

Two more registries, for the Label-Index TLV flags and the Originator SRGB TLV flags, start empty with 16-bit flag fields and Expert Review. The designated experts are asked to scrutinize flag requests closely, and no single use case should need more than one flag bit.
sections.eli5: The rule book keeps a list of which kind of box has which number. Two kinds are taken, one old number is retired, and the rest are saved for later.

sections.title: Manageability and Security
sections.content:
The attribute is meant to stay within one SR or administrative domain, which may include several ASes. By default it SHOULD NOT be attached or advertised, so advertisement requires explicit enablement, and propagation to other ASes MUST be explicitly configured.

The security considerations inherit those of RFC 4271, RFC 8277 and RFC 8402. With BGPsec (RFC 8205) the attribute adds no unique concerns, but it is not protected by the BGPsec signatures. Operators are expected to filter it at the domain boundary so internal prefix and topology information does not leak.

To limit denial-of-service from floods of updates carrying invalid or conflicting attributes, error log rate limiting and suppression of duplicate messages SHOULD be deployed.
sections.eli5: These signposts are for the home neighborhood only, so the router keeps them off the public road and does not shout the same complaint over and over.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value portion in octets.

fields.name: RESERVED
fields.desc: Clear on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: None defined; clear on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: Label Index
fields.desc: Index value in the SRGB space.

items.label: Label-Index
items.desc: Carries the label index for the prefix.

items.label: Deprecated
items.desc: Formerly the IPv6 SID TLV from earlier drafts.

items.label: Originator SRGB
items.desc: Carries the SRGB of the originating node.
